sections.title: Scene 3: The Chapel of Saint Vey

npcs.name: Rill Fenwick
npcs.motivation: Rill wants the harbour conservancy to stop blaming the ferrymen and will help anyone who clears them.

npcs.name: Sister Osmund
npcs.motivation: Sister Osmund wants the bell's midnight ringing explained before the chapel's repute suffers.

npcs.name: Keeper Dain
npcs.motivation: Keeper Dain wants the tide gate left alone and the bell mystery forgotten.

secrets.text: A tidal bellows drives the harbour bell through a rope frame, so the bell rings whenever the tide gate opens, with no one at the tower.
Sister Osmund sends a youthful apprentice to fetch the salt water, and the small footprints are his, pacing the tide gate schedule.
The archive copy of the tide schedule proves the bell frame was raised by the conservancy itself, and never by a hand.
The crypt tally was cut by the apprentices of the conservancy to mark the bell's test strokes, one for each night.

sceneConditions.condition: If the party asks about the bell here, Rill says the bell was struck at midnight on three nights running and points them toward the tidemill.
If the party examines the rope, they notice it was cut from above at head height rather than worn through.
If the party searches the chapel, they find the sexton's old coat hanging on a nail, still smelling of fish oil.
If the party breaks the ward by force, the bell rings once, wildly, and every ferryman in the harbour looks up at the tower.

branch.description: A side path to the tide archive that yields the tide schedule and a hint toward the crypt door, and can be skipped without blocking the ending.

alternativeSolution.description: Name the bellows and the tide gate to the ward, or show the archive tide schedule, instead of battering the warded door down.

missableClue.clue: The ledger records boats in the harbour at midnight, and the bell time matches the tide gate.

conclusions.statement: The bell was rung by the tidal bellows, not by a person.

clues.text: Fresh salt spray covers the wheel chamber, though the tower stands a quarter mile away.
The rope hangs freshly cut above a man's head height, rather than worn through.
Salt water fills the bellows, though the bellows are supposed to blow air.
Drops of clean salt water mark small wet footprints between the chapel and the tidemill.
The archive copy of the tide schedule shows the bell frame was raised to warn ships.

testimonies.claim: The sexton struck the bell with his own hand at midnight.
testimonies.canonicalFact: The sexton died five winters ago; the bell was rung by the tidal bellows.

testimonies.claim: I closed the tide gate before midnight.
testimonies.canonicalFact: The keeper closed the gate, but an apprentice reopened it to run the bellows.

endings.description: The tidal bellows are proven, the conservancy is named, and the harbour accepts the truth.
The party leaves without proof and the bellows are cut; the conservancy seals the tower and the ferrymen are blamed.
